PullRequest.Title: sessions: polish: add new session button treatments
PullRequest.Body:
## Summary

Adds two lighter New Session button treatments while preserving the current rendering as the control:

- a flat shortcut using the button label typography;
- the same lightweight shortcut on a subtle grouped background.

All three options are available through one hidden, experiment-backed setting so the treatments can be compared without exposing a user-facing preference.

## Context

The Agents Window shares `NewSessionActionViewItem` between the Sessions sidebar header and the experiment-gated Agents title bar. The current button renders its shortcut as a small monospace chip inside the outlined button, which gives the action a visually heavy nested-control appearance.

The redesigned shortcut must also account for platform conventions: macOS renders `⌘N`, while Windows renders the longer `Ctrl+N` chord. This PR therefore keeps the current treatment and adds two alternatives rather than selecting a replacement prematurely.

## Implementation

The shared compact-button renderer now exposes a small configuration hook. One contribution-owned observable resolves the presentation, and every New Session action reads it to apply modifier classes to the existing VS Code `Button`; command behavior, telemetry, accessibility, keybinding resolution, and onboarding remain on the existing path.

The lightweight base treatment:

- inherits the button label's UI font, line height, and foreground, while using the quieter `label2` type role;
- removes the nested keycap border, radius, padding, and background;
- keeps platform-native chord notation from `KeybindingLabel`.

The background treatment adds a subtle surface around the complete shortcut using existing keybinding-label colors and design tokens.

Because hidden settings are excluded from automatic experimental-default processing, the contribution explicitly resolves the treatment. It observes configuration changes and assignment refetches, gives an explicitly configured developer value precedence, and updates the shared style observable. Already-rendered sidebar and title-bar buttons react without a reload.

## Experiment and developer override

The hidden application-scoped `sessions.newSessionButton.style` setting supports:

| Value | Presentation |
|---|---|
| `default` | Existing small monospace keybinding chip |
| `lightweight` | Flat shortcut using the button label typography |
| `lightweightWithKeybindingBackground` | Lightweight typography with a subtle grouped background |

The exact ExP treatment key is **`agentSessionsNewSessionButtonStyle`**; use that string as written with one of the three values above. It is resolved initially and on assignment refetch.

The setting defaults to `default` and is excluded from the normal Settings UI. An explicit `sessions.newSessionButton.style` value in settings JSON takes precedence over the ExP treatment.

## Platform behavior

The button continues to use the resolved command keybinding:

- macOS renders `⌘N`;
- Windows renders `Ctrl+N`;
- Linux follows its resolved platform label;
- user remappings, hover text, and localized ARIA labels remain intact.

## Visual comparison

![Original, flat, and subtle-background New Session button treatments on macOS and Windows](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/a75ab87e-5cc1-489d-918f-f17b7fa750f8)

## Visual coverage

Two button-only component fixtures render the production New Session action without the Automations row:

- lightweight without a keybinding background;
- lightweight with a subtle grouped background.

Each fixture runs in Light, Dark, and Dark High Contrast themes. One fixture exercises a post-render settings override, while the other exercises the explicit ExP treatment path. Existing Automations fixtures continue to cover the default treatment.

## Validation

- ESLint passed for the changed TypeScript and fixture files.
- Stylelint passed for the changed CSS.
- Component Explorer rendered all six redesigned theme variants successfully.
- Windows user-agent emulation confirmed `Ctrl+N` and the `New Session (Control+N)` accessible label.
- `git diff --check` passed.

Scenarios.Scenario: Workbench startup/restore creates NewSessionActionViewItemContribution and resolves the button style
Scenarios.CriticalPath: The BlockRestore constructor synchronously creates observables/listeners and schedules updateNewSessionButtonStyle, but does not await it; restore and initial button rendering can proceed with the default style. The async treatment result and class update are off the startup critical path.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Initialize the shared TAS client and perform or await its initial assignments fetch.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One shared client/fetch per assignment-service setup; the new style read joins that existing fetch rather than issuing one request per button or treatment.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: This same contribution already injected the delayed assignment service and called updateTitleBarTreatment at construction, which instantiated the service and started the shared TAS client/fetch.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: The changed constructor launches the style read without awaiting it, so this fetch does not block contribution construction, restore, or initial rendering.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Serialize the treatment result and enqueue a tasClientReadTreatmentComplete telemetry event.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One additional event for the style lookup at startup when no explicit style is configured.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Only the pre-existing title-bar treatment read emitted its corresponding treatment-read event; there was no style-treatment event.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Runs after the asynchronous treatment read and is not awaited by restore or button rendering.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: Constant per workbench contribution instance, independent of session count; rendered button count does not multiply treatment reads.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: The style read may overlap the existing title-bar treatment read, but both share one TAS client and initial fetch; no per-button requests are created.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: Cold startup may await the assignment service's one shared initial fetch; warm reads resolve from the initialized TAS client's in-memory assignments. An explicit developer setting bypasses getTreatment entirely.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: constructor call flow, non-awaited async scheduling, and shared assignment-service implementation were directly inspected.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Exact TAS initialization and telemetry enqueue cost varies by platform and cache state, but the added work is constant and off the critical path.
Scenarios.Verdict: No reportable regression: the diff adds one bounded cached treatment read and telemetry event without adding a network fetch or blocking startup.

Scenarios.Scenario: User changes sessions.newSessionButton.style while sidebar/title-bar buttons are mounted
Scenarios.CriticalPath: The key-filtered configuration observable reruns the contribution autorun, inspect finds the explicit value, and the shared observable synchronously toggles two classes on each mounted New Session button. No layout read or forced synchronous relayout is performed.
Scenarios.ScalingInput: At most the sidebar and experiment-gated title-bar action instances; independent of session-list size.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: One autorun update, followed synchronously by at most two button autoruns; no queue, IPC, filesystem, database, subprocess, or network work.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: Explicit configuration takes precedence and bypasses the assignment service. Re-setting the same normalized observable value does not create additional downstream style work beyond observable semantics.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: registration sites, observable filtering, and class-only DOM writes were directly inspected.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: The exact number of mounted buttons is UI-state dependent but bounded by the two registered menu surfaces.
Scenarios.Verdict: No reportable regression: constant bounded DOM class updates with no geometry reads or expensive boundary.

Scenarios.Scenario: Experiment assignments refetch while New Session controls are present
Scenarios.CriticalPath: After the assignment service completes its own refetch and emits onDidRefetchAssignments, the contribution performs one style getTreatment and the pre-existing title-bar getTreatment. Style changes propagate to mounted controls, but product interaction does not wait for either read.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Refresh all TAS assignments before onDidRefetchAssignments is emitted.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One service-level refetch per filter/poll trigger, shared by all consumers.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Assignment-service polling/filter changes already performed this shared refetch and the contribution already reread the title-bar treatment afterward.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: The network operation precedes the event consumed by this diff and is not introduced or multiplied by the style listener.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Serialize and enqueue one telemetry event for the newly reread style treatment.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One additional style event per assignment-refetch event, not per button or session.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The refetch already caused the title-bar treatment reread/event, but not the style-treatment reread/event.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: No user workflow waits for it; class updates occur after the cached read.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: Assignment-refetch event frequency, not session or button cardinality; effective style lookup cardinality is one per event.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: One style promise and one existing title-bar promise may run together; the request counter discards stale style results if events overlap, while underlying reads remain cached.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: The refetch has completed before the signal fires, so getTreatment reads the updated in-memory assignment cache. Explicit style configuration still bypasses the treatment read.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: event ordering and assignment-service cache/network implementation were directly inspected.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Refetch frequency is externally controlled, but normal polling/filter events are infrequent and each added read is constant.
Scenarios.Verdict: No reportable regression: no new network fan-out, unbounded burst, or button-count multiplier.

Scenarios.Scenario: Render and dispose the shared New Session action in sidebar and optional title bar
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Rendering registers one autorun per action that reads the contribution-wide style and writes two class toggles. Disposing the action disposes the autorun through the view item's Disposable registration.
Scenarios.ScalingInput: One autorun per rendered action, bounded to the two registered menu surfaces.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Synchronous constant-time class writes on render/style changes; no asynchronous fan-out.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: All actions share the single already-resolved observable; no per-action cache or treatment read exists.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: renderer ownership, registration, and disposal were directly inspected.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Whether both surfaces are simultaneously mounted depends on the title-bar experiment, but the upper bound remains two.
Scenarios.Verdict: No reportable regression: bounded listeners and correct cleanup prevent retained controls or lifecycle growth.

Analysis.Summary: Completed the performance pass over all five changed files and every diff hunk. Traced startup, configuration override, assignment refetch, button render/update, disposal, shared TAS network/cache behavior, telemetry serialization, and effective UI cardinality. No high-confidence actionable performance regression was introduced, and the PR does not itself fix a concrete shipped performance regression.
